Reading · three festivals, three kinds of tired

1.1 Discuss. Have you ever been to a music festival? What is the best thing about live music — and the worst?

KEY WORDS

a line-up the list of who is playing

a headliner the most famous act

a stage where the musicians perform

a queue a line of people waiting

Three Festivals, Three Kinds of Tired

THE BIG ONE. This is the festival whose line-up you already know, because it was announced in January and argued about until June. Eighty thousand people, six stages, and a headliner who comes on at eleven. The sound is extraordinary and the organisation is faultless. What nobody tells you is that you will walk fifteen kilometres a day, and that the act you most wanted to see is playing at the same time as the other act you most wanted to see. You go home exhausted and slightly disappointed, and you book again in November.

THE SMALL ONE. Four hundred people in a field, which is run by a family who have done it for nineteen years. Nobody has heard of any of the musicians, which is the point. You can stand two metres from a stage where somebody is playing something you have never heard before, and afterwards you can talk to them, because they are queuing behind you for coffee. The organisers' great achievement is not the music but the atmosphere: everybody behaves well, because everybody can see everybody else.

THE FREE ONE. A city square, three afternoons in September, no tickets and no fence. This is the festival where you meet your neighbours, which sounds sentimental until it happens. The performances are shorter and the quality varies, but there is a particular pleasure in watching a seventy-year-old accordion player who has an audience of two hundred strangers and clearly did not expect one. The tiredness afterwards is the good kind, and it costs nothing.

Three quite different experiences of the same thing, then. The mistake is to assume the biggest must be the best — that is a statement about money, not about music.

2

Grammar · defining and non-defining relative clauses

PRESENTATION

A relative clause adds information about a noun. There are two kinds, and the difference is not decoration — it changes the meaning.

D Defining — tells you which one. Without it you do not know what the speaker means. The festival that we went to in June was tiny. · That's the DJ who was here two weeks ago. No commas.

ND Non-defining — you already know which one; this is extra information. Glastonbury, which is most famous as a music festival, also has theatre and comedy. Two commas — one each side.

→ The pronouns. who = a person · which / that = a thing · whose = belonging to · where = a place · when = a time

You can leave the pronoun out — but only in a defining clause, and only when it is the object: I downloaded a song (that) you'll like. · The music (which) I chose was wrong. Never in a non-defining clause.

Defining — no commas

Non-defining — two commas

My brother who lives in Almaty is a DJ. (I have more than one brother.)

My brother, who lives in Almaty, is a DJ. (I have one brother.)

The songs that were written in 1969 still sell.

Auld Lang Syne, which was written by Robert Burns, is sung all over the world.

that and which are both fine.

which only — never that.

The pronoun can disappear if it is the object.

The pronoun can never disappear.

ERROR WARNING

Three mistakes, and the second is the one that survives longest:

1 what instead of that / which. Here's the information what you asked for. ✗ → the information that / which you asked for ✓

2 The missing comma. We stayed at the Palace Hotel which is right next to the beach. ✗ → the Palace Hotel, which is right next to the beach ✓ Without the comma you are saying there are several Palace Hotels and you mean the seaside one.

3 that or what in a non-defining clause. I finally went to the USA, that I had always dreamed of visiting. ✗ → the USA, which I had always dreamed of visiting ✓

PRONUNCIATION — THE COMMA YOU CAN HEAR

A non-defining clause is said with a pause at each comma, and the voice drops slightly inside it. A defining clause runs straight through with no pause at all.

My brother who lives in Almaty is a DJ. → no pause: one of several brothers.

My brother | who lives in Almaty | is a DJ. → two pauses: the brother, and by the way he lives in Almaty.

This is the only signal a listener gets. Say both versions to a class and ask how many brothers? — the answers will split, and that is the lesson.

PRESENTATION

The music set: an album · an audience · a choir · a DJ · a festival · an instrument · a musician · an orchestra · a playlist · a track · to perform · to play live

PRONUNCIATION — THE STRESS MOVES

Adding an ending often moves the stress, and students keep the old one. That is the single most common reason a correct word is not understood.

MUsic → muSICian · CELebrate → celeBRAtion · CREative → creaTIVity

BEAUtiful → BEAUty · HAPpy → HAPpiness · CULtural → CULture (these keep it)

The rule that covers most of it: -ion, -ity and -ian pull the stress onto the syllable immediately before the ending. -ness, -ty and -ment leave it where it was.

A small festival is not a smaller version of a big one; it is a different thing. The (1 organise) is usually one family, and the (2 perform) they book are people nobody has heard of. CONTRASTING IDEAS

Five ways to say but, and they are not interchangeable — what follows each one is different.

however + a new sentence. I was given free tickets. However, I don't like that music.

although / while + a clause (subject + verb). Although TV screens have got bigger, there's nothing like a cinema.

despite / in spite of + a noun or an -ing form — never a clause. Despite my love of special effects, I still want a good story. · In spite of the convenience of watching at home, I prefer the cinema.

Careful: Despite it was expensive ✗ → Although it was expensive ✓ or Despite the cost ✓. And however takes a comma, not a full stop before it: I like it however it's long ✗.

5.4 Read the model article, then answer.

MODEL

Why I Stopped Going to the Cinema

I love films. I love going out with friends. So why do I now watch almost everything at home?

The first reason is the other people. Cinema is supposed to be a social experience, and in theory I agree. However, the last time I went, a couple behind me laughed loudly at things that were not funny, and continued talking after I asked them to stop. Despite the enormous screen, I spent two hours listening to them instead of the film.

The second reason is control. Although it sounds lazy, being able to pause a film matters to me. If something is disappointing, I can stop. In spite of what people say about attention spans, I think choosing when to stop is a sign of respect for your own time, not a lack of it.

While I still miss the darkness and the size, then, I have made my choice. The cinema gave me a room full of strangers. Home gives me the film.

4 Does the conclusion add a new idea? What does it do instead?

HOW TO BUILD THE ARTICLE

Paragraph 1 — the hook. State your position, or ask the reader a question. Short.

Paragraph 2 — reason one, with an example that actually happened.

Paragraph 3 — reason two, and here is where you answer the objection somebody would make.

Paragraph 4 — the conclusion. Summarise, and close with something that stays in the head. Do not add a new idea here — that is the commonest structural fault at this level.
